newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila investors upbeat despite political row.
newsitem.headline: Manila investors upbeat despite political row.

text.p: The Philippines remains attractive to foreign investors despite a political row over moves to extend President Fidel Ramos' term, business leaders said.
"The interest in the country today is very high," Peter Wallace, president of consultancy firm Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) Philippines, said at the weekend.

Many investors had put the Philippines on top of the list of the most exciting investment prospects in Asia, Wallace said at the close of discussions between Philippine government officials and foreign businessmen.
Participants at the conference mentioned China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, India and Taiwan as other countries in which they were interested, Wallace said.
"We are convinced that the (Philippine) economy has turned the corner ... from its boom and bust cycle," Wallace said.
"The only flies in the ointment are the political transition in 1998 ... and (questions on) the Filipino First policy," he added.
A controversy brewing for several months over whether President Fidel Ramos would seek to run for a second term in the 1998 elections came to a head last week.

Ramos has consistently said he would step down next year in line with a constitutional provision fixing a president's term at six years without re-election -- a limitation designed to curb ambitions by anyone seeking to follow the path of deposed late President Ferdinand Marcos.
But Ramos' sincerety was questioned when members of his Lakas (People Power) party said they favoured lifting the limit and believed they could convince the president.
The issue has polarised the nation as his supporters have begun gathering signatures to force the holding of a plebiscite to amend the charter.
But this did not concern foreign investors, Wallace said.
"Whoever is chosen, we don't care. What we want to see is policy consistency," Wallace said.
Hoewver, local brokerage Anscor Hagedorn Securities said the country's image would be sullied if the political wranglings continued over extensions to the presidential term.
"The economic turnaround (Ramos) so carefully engineered will be for naught if the country loses the faith of the international community," it said in a research paper.

Wallace said foreign investors were concerned about the February 3 decision of the Supreme Court, voiding the sale of historic Manila Hotel to Malaysian infrastructure firm Renong Berhad after a successful bid by public tender.
The court's decision followed a petition by the losing bidder, Manila Prince Hotel Corporation, which later offered to match the Malaysian firm's bid.
The court, citing a "Filipino First Policy", upheld Manila Prince's contention that the Manila Hotel was part of the country's heritage and should not be sold to a foreign group.
"We all understand national patrimony but this issue should have been decided before, not after (the bidding)," Wallace said.
